summary: This standards-track document extends DHCP so that a relay agent may use any available source port for upstream communications, rather than a fixed one. The extension also includes a DHCP option that lets responses be routed back to the right port statelessly. This helps in cases where a fixed port is awkward to use.

plainLanguage.summary: A messenger normally uses the same door each time. This lets the messenger use any free door and leaves a note so replies find the right one.

questions: can a dhcp relay use any source port
how do dhcp responses return to a relay source port
what is the dhcp relay source port option
why upgrade the dhcp server before relays
subtitle: Lets a DHCP relay agent send from any UDP source port and still get replies routed back to it.

tldr.problem: DHCP relay agents had to use the fixed well-known UDP port as their source port, which is awkward when relay work is split across several processes that share one IP address.
tldr.mechanism: A relay may use any non-DHCP source port. The server replies to whatever port the message came from, and in DHCPv6 cascades a new Relay Source Port Option records the downstream relay's port so replies can find their way back without relay state.
tldr.outcome: Both the server and any upstream relay must support the extension, so servers should be upgraded before relays, and firewall rules that match fixed source ports may need changes.

today: RFC 8357 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Fixed Relay Port Is a Problem
sections.content:
RFC 2131 and RFC 3315 run DHCP over UDP and fix the port numbers. For IPv4 the server port is 67 and the client port is 68. For IPv6 the server port is 547 and the client port is 546.

That fixed pairing causes trouble in large relay deployments. A single switch may split its DHCP relay work across several processes that all share one IP address. If the UDP source port must be a fixed number, all DHCP packets would have to pass through one central process, which defeats the point of distributing the work. Giving each process its own IP address is possible but adds operational and management complexity, especially given the scarcity of IPv4 addresses.

This RFC relaxes the fixed source port rule for relay agents. The server must remember the UDP port of each incoming packet along with the address, and reply to that port instead of the fixed DHCP port.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine every helper in a post office had to use the very same mailbox slot. They would queue up and get in each other's way. This lets each helper use their own slot.

sections.title: Terms Used for Relay Ports
sections.content:
The RFC defines a few port terms for chains of relays. An upstream device is the next relay agent or server that receives Relay-forward messages. A downstream device is the next relay agent that receives Relay-reply messages.

  • Relay Source Port: the UDP port a relay agent uses to receive Relay-forward messages from an upstream device.
  • Downstream Source Port: the UDP port the downstream device used when forwarding to this relay. This relay uses it when sending Relay-reply messages back to that device.
  • Non-DHCP UDP Port: any valid, non-zero UDP port other than 67 for DHCPv4 and 547 for DHCPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: Upstream is the way toward the boss, and downstream is the way back toward the person who asked. A port is just the number of the door a message uses.

sections.title: The Sub-option and the Option
sections.content:
Relays keep no state, so a relay that does not use the standard port must put the needed port information into the message itself. Two new items carry it.

For DHCPv4, the Source Port Sub-option lives inside the Relay Agent Information option from RFC 3046. It has an 8-bit code of 19 and an 8-bit length that is set to 0, so it carries no data.

For DHCPv6, the Relay Source Port Option has option code 135 (OPTION_RELAY_PORT) and a length of 2. Its one field, Downstream Source Port, is 16 bits. The relay sets it to the downstream relay's UDP source port, or to zero if only the local relay uses a non-DHCP port.
sections.plainLanguage: The DHCPv4 version is a tiny flag that says I am using a different door. The DHCPv6 version is a note that also writes down the door number.

sections.title: Relay Agent and Server Behavior
sections.content:
In DHCPv4, a relay that uses a non-DHCP port (not 67) MUST include the Source Port Sub-option in the messages it forwards. A server that sees the sub-option MUST remember the UDP source port of the message and use it as the destination port when replying to that relay.

In DHCPv6, a relay MUST include the Relay Source Port Option in three cases: the local relay uses a non-DHCP port (not 547), the downstream relay does, or both do. When only the local relay uses such a port, Downstream Source Port is zero. Otherwise it holds the port the downstream relay used.

The DHCPv6 server MUST copy the option into the Relay-reply chain, MUST check and use the UDP source port of the Relay-forward packet when replying, and the option MUST NOT appear in any message other than Relay-forward or Relay-reply. A relay that gets a Relay-reply with a non-zero Downstream Source Port MUST use that port when forwarding to the downstream relay.
sections.plainLanguage: The reply goes back to the same door the question came from. If there are several helpers in a chain, each one leaves a note saying which door the previous helper used.

sections.title: A Cascaded IPv6 Relay Example
sections.content:
The RFC walks through three chained relays and a server. Relay1 is the only one using a non-DHCP port, 1000. Relay2 is upstream of Relay1 and supports the extension. Relay3 does not support it.

Relay1 includes the option with Downstream Source Port set to zero. Relay2 notices the option and sees the packet came from port 1000, so it includes its own option with the field set to 1000. The server copies the option into its Relay-reply. Relay2 reads 1000 and sends the reply to Relay1 on that port. Relay1 sees zero and uses the normal port 547 toward a downstream relay, or 546 toward a client.

The RFC states that this works with any combination of cascaded relays, as long as the relay using the non-DHCP port and its upstream device support the extension.
sections.plainLanguage: Relay2 writes on a sticky note that the question came through door 1000. When the answer returns, the note tells Relay2 where to hand it back.

sections.title: Compatibility and Deployment
sections.content:
Sites that want relays with custom source ports need new software on both the DHCP server and the relay agents. If only the relay is upgraded, the server cannot talk back to it. Operators should therefore upgrade the server first. If the upstream relay or server lacks the extension, the relay port feature needs to be disabled.

The default relay behavior should remain the DHCP UDP port, and the RFC recommends that configuration allow a mode where a non-DHCP port may be used.

Firewalls that match both a static source and destination port may stop matching the new traffic. Their rules need to match only the DHCP server side port number and, if necessary, IP addresses and other attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides need to learn the new trick before it works, so teach the receiver first. Also, any guard who checks door numbers needs new instructions.

sections.title: Security and IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The security section is short. It points to RFC 3118 and RFC 3315 for the threats of using DHCP and says this extension does not raise additional security issues.

IANA has registered the DHCPv4 Relay Source Port Sub-option (19) in the Relay Agent Information option sub-option registry, and OPTION_RELAY_PORT (135) in the DHCPv6 option codes registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors say the new trick does not open any new holes, and the new numbers have been written in the official list.

fields.name: Downstream Source Port
fields.desc: Downstream relay's UDP source port, or zero if only the local relay uses a non-DHCP port.

messages.label: Relay-forward, option = 1000
messages.note: Relay2 records the port it saw.
